title: Inside BlogerMenia: How This Platform Actually Works
subtitle: A full tour of the system you are reading this on — two apps, one contract, and an AI search index that keeps itself honest.
introduction: Most "our architecture" posts stop at a box diagram. This one goes all the way down. BlogerMenia is a headless blogging platform: a Next.js app owns everything a reader or writer sees, a Django REST Framework API owns the data, the identity and the AI, and the two only ever meet over HTTP. That split sounds simple until you ask the awkward questions — who holds the tokens, what happens when Gemini is down, how does a post get into a vector index, and who pays for it when someone hammers the search box. This post answers all of them with the real code and the real reasoning, including the bugs that shaped each decision.
conclusion: Nothing in this system is clever for its own sake. Every rule in it — the API client that is the only file allowed to call Django, the selector that must change whenever a serializer does, the content hash that stops a re-save from paying for an embedding twice, the single-use code that keeps a JWT out of the browser's history — exists because the alternative failed in a way that was hard to see. That is the through-line: the architecture is not optimised for looking impressive, it is optimised for making failures visible. A post that never reached the search index says so in the admin. A search outage returns 503 instead of an empty list. A save that raced another author's save gets a 409 instead of quietly winning. Build for the day it breaks, and the day it works takes care of itself.

sections.title: 1. The shape of the system
sections.content:
BlogerMenia runs as two independent services.

The Next.js app is the entire user-facing surface: routing, rendering, SEO, forms, the editor, the session. It is deployed on its own and can be restarted without touching the data.

The Django app is an API and nothing else. It renders no blog pages, ships no blog templates, and has no context processors. `Blog.get_absolute_url()` returns a URL on the frontend, built from the `FRONTEND_URL` setting — reversing a Django route there would raise `NoReverseMatch`, because no such route exists.

There is exactly one exception, and it is deliberate: `/accounts/` is django-allauth's own view tree, kept alive because the LinkedIn OAuth redirect dance has to terminate on Django. Next.js proxies to it. Section 6 explains how identity crosses back.

sections.title: 2. The frontend is a BFF, not a client
sections.content:
The most consequential frontend decision: the browser has no data layer. It cannot call Django, and it does not know Django's address.

Everything flows through the Next.js server. Server Components fetch directly. Anything the browser needs to trigger — logging in, posting a contact form, running a search — goes to a route handler under `app/api/`, which does the real call server-side. That is the Backend-For-Frontend pattern, and three properties fall out of it for free:

Tokens live in httpOnly cookies that no script can read, ours or an injected one. CORS needs no configuration at all, because there is no cross-origin request to permit — `CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS` is `False` and stays that way. And the client bundle ships zero API-calling code, so nothing about the backend's surface is discoverable from the browser.

sections.title: The one file allowed to talk to Django

sections.content: The `import "server-only"` line at the top of that file is load-bearing. It turns "a client component must never import the data layer" from a code-review convention into a build error. The same guard sits on the config module, the cookie module and the session module.

sections.title: 3. Authentication: bearer tokens the browser cannot see
sections.content:
Django issues a SimpleJWT access/refresh pair. Login is `POST /api/v1/auth/login/` with an email and password — `ACCOUNT_LOGIN_METHODS` is `{"email"}`, so email is the credential, not a username.

What is unusual is where the tokens go. Not `localStorage`, not a JS-readable cookie, not a header the client manages. The Next.js route handler receives them and writes two httpOnly cookies, `bm_access` and `bm_refresh`, both `SameSite=Lax` and `Secure` in production. `SameSite=Lax` is what protects the mutating route handlers from CSRF: the browser will not attach those cookies to a cross-site POST.

Server Components cannot set cookies, which creates one wrinkle worth naming. When the access cookie has lapsed, `getViewer()` simply reads as signed-out during that render — it cannot silently refresh. `POST /api/auth/session` is the route that does the refresh and writes the new cookie, and the client calls it on mount.

sections.title: 4. The backend, in four layers
sections.content:
Every Django app here has the same shape, and the shape is enforced rather than suggested. There is one naming rule that catches people first: **DRF views live in `api.py` or an `api/` package — never `views.py`.** These are API endpoints, not Django template views, and the filename should say so.

There is exactly one documented exception, `linkedin_oidc/views.py`, because django-allauth resolves a provider's OAuth views by importing the literal path `<package>.views.oauth2_login`. Rename the module and social login breaks at import time. The file carries a comment saying so.

sections.title: The selector/serializer contract that keeps list endpoints fast
sections.content:
# blog/selectors.py — the read queryset annotates what the serializer will read
queryset.annotate(like_count_annotated=Count('likes', distinct=True))


# blog/serializers/ — reads the annotation; falls back only off the hot path
def get_like_count(self, obj) -> int:
    annotated = getattr(obj, 'like_count_annotated', None)
    return annotated if annotated is not None else obj.likes.count()

# A SerializerMethodField that queries unconditionally is an N+1 per row.
# The serializer and the selector are changed together, or not at all.

Pro tip that cost this project real bugs: `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` only asks whether the caller is signed in — never whether the object is theirs. Every writable detail view needs an object permission beside it: `permission_classes = [IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly, IsAuthorOrReadOnly]`. And filter the detail queryset too, because `Model.objects.all()` on a `Retrieve` view publishes drafts to anyone who can guess a slug — and slugs come from titles.

sections.title: 5. Concurrent edits get a 409, not a silent overwrite
sections.content:
Two people editing the same post is not a hypothetical on a platform with playlists and co-authors. The default REST behaviour — last write wins — throws away one person's work with no trace.

`OptimisticLockMixin` fixes that without a lock table. The client echoes back the `updated_at` it last saw as `expected_updated_at`. If the stored value has moved on, someone saved in between and this write would discard their edit, so it raises `409 Conflict` with a message a human can act on. Clients that omit the field keep the old behaviour, which makes the whole thing backwards compatible.

sections.title: core/mixins.py
6. Social login: carrying identity across a boundary
sections.content:
This is the trickiest flow in the system, and it is worth walking through slowly.

The LinkedIn OAuth dance has to run against Django — allauth owns the redirect URLs and LinkedIn has one registered callback. But it *ends* in a Django session, and the Next.js app authenticates with JWT cookies it sets itself. Something has to carry the identity across that boundary.

The obvious approach is to put the token pair in the callback's redirect URL. It works, and it also writes both tokens into the browser's history, the referrer of the next request, and every proxy log in between.

So the redirect carries a **single-use code** instead, and the frontend redeems it server-to-server for the real tokens. The codes live in the cache rather than a table: they are valid for sixty seconds and there is nothing worth keeping once redeemed.

sections.title: accounts/services/social_handoff.py
sections.content:
TTL_SECONDS = 60          # survives exactly one browser round trip
_PREFIX = "social-handoff:"


def issue_code(user) -> str:
    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    cache.set(f"{_PREFIX}{code}", user.pk, TTL_SECONDS)
    return code


def redeem_code(code: str):
    """The user `code` was issued for, or None. Single use: the code dies here.

    Deleting *before* the user lookup means a code cannot be replayed even if
    two requests arrive at once.
    """
    key = f"{_PREFIX}{code}"
    user_pk = cache.get(key)
    if user_pk is None:
        return None
    cache.delete(key)
    return get_user_model().objects.filter(pk=user_pk, is_active=True).first()

sections.title: 7. Content: posts are structured blocks, not a blob of HTML
sections.content:
A blog post here is not one rich-text field. `Blog` carries a `sections` JSON column: an ordered list of typed blocks, alongside `introduction`, `conclusion`, `subtitle`, `excerpt` and `tags`.

That choice pays off in four places at once. The renderer switches on `section.type`, so a code block gets real syntax highlighting and a table gets its own horizontally-scrolling container on a phone. The table of contents is derived from section titles rather than scraped from the DOM. Reading time is computed from the fields — deliberately skipping code blocks, which are skimmed, not read at prose speed. And the search index can build meaningful text out of a post whose legacy `content` field is empty.

The old single `content` field is still there and still rendered for older posts; `isStructured()` decides which path a given post takes.

sections.title: What a post actually looks like on the wire

sections.content: Two traps live in this model. First, DRF stores a multipart JSON string verbatim and treats an absent boolean as `False` — the unchecked-checkbox convention — so `sections` and every flag go through `core.fields.JSONListField` and `core.fields.BooleanField`. Second, author-supplied markup is sanitised on write (`clean_html` for content, `clean_svg` for Excalidraw data) *and* again on render. Neither layer is sufficient alone.

sections.title: 8. Semantic search: the write path
sections.content:
Search here matches on meaning, not keywords. Blogs, playlists and author profiles are all embedded into the same Milvus collection under stable document ids like `blog:12`.

Embedding is a paid, network-bound call to Gemini, so it never happens inside a request. A `post_save` signal schedules the work on `transaction.on_commit` — the author's save returns immediately, and the worker only ever sees committed rows.

The signal also diffs `update_fields` against a set of indexed fields before scheduling anything. That check exists because `SIMPLE_JWT.UPDATE_LAST_LOGIN` writes `last_login` on every token issue, which fires `User.post_save`: the system used to re-embed a full profile every single time somebody signed in.

sections.title: search/tasks.py — the task that decides whether to spend money
9. Semantic search: the read path
sections.content:
A reader types in the header search box. The client debounces, hits `GET /api/search?q=…` on the BFF, which calls Django's `/api/v1/search/`.

Django embeds the query — with an instruction prefix, because `gemini-embedding-001` is trained for asymmetric retrieval, where the *query* carries an instruction and indexed documents stay plain. Milvus then finds the nearest vectors under a **cosine** metric. That metric matters: the default L2 made the `min_score` threshold meaningless, since Gemini's embeddings are normalised and cosine is the only metric those relevance scores are valid for.

The matches come back as `(score, kind, object_id)` tuples, and Django loads the real model instances with `in_bulk()` to render them. `is_published` is re-checked at read time, not just at index time — a post unpublished after indexing would otherwise stay searchable until the next sweep.

sections.title: The instructed query embedding
Search is the one read endpoint that costs money — so it is fenced in
items: Queries shorter than 2 characters return an empty list without touching Gemini.
Results are cached for 5 minutes under a sha256 of the lowercased query — identical searches used to pay for identical embeddings.
The endpoint is throttled to 30 requests a minute via a dedicated `search` scope.
Results below a 0.1 relevance score are dropped rather than padding the list with noise.

A failure returns 503 with a real message. Returning 200 and an empty list — which is what this used to do — makes an outage indistinguishable from "no matches", so nobody finds out search has been broken for a week.

sections.title: 10. Background work, and the one retry policy
sections.content:
Every third-party call in the system runs on Celery: embedding, Gemini excerpt and tag generation, and LinkedIn shares.

There used to be three different retry policies — five retries with backoff in `search`, three in `blog`, a hand-rolled flat 60-second `self.retry` in `accounts`, and none at all on the delete path. Worse, all of them retried bare `Exception`, so a task that could never succeed — a post with no text to embed — still burned its entire retry budget against a paid API.

Now there is one policy in `core/tasks.py`, and two exception types that carry the decision: `TransientError` for something worth trying again, `PermanentError` for something that will fail identically forever. A `classify()` helper maps the untyped garbage that Gemini and Milvus raise onto those two, by looking for markers like `timeout`, `rate limit`, `resource_exhausted` and `503`.

sections.title: Two scheduled jobs, both there to clean up after failure
items: **Every 6 hours — reindex pending embeddings.** Re-embeds anything whose `embedding_status` is not `indexed`: a task that failed, or a save that happened while the broker was down. It reads the ids already in Milvus first, so the sweep is incremental. That check used to be `hasattr(store, 'get')` — a ChromaDB API. Milvus has no `get`, so it was always False, the "only index what's missing" path silently became a full rebuild, and every sweep re-embedded the entire corpus against a paid API.

**Every 24 hours — prune orphaned embeddings.** Deletes vectors whose backing row is gone, covering deletes that happened while Milvus was unreachable. Necessary because result resolution silently drops ids it cannot load, which makes an orphan invisible rather than error-producing.

sections.title: 11. Caching that cannot go stale
sections.content:
The category list is read on every page render and carries per-category post counts. A TTL is the wrong tool here: too long and a newly created category takes an hour to appear, too short and it may as well be uncached.

So each cached family carries a version counter. Keys are derived from it, and a content save bumps the version — which orphans every key in that family at once. No invalidation bookkeeping, and no window where a reader sees last hour's data.

sections.title: 12. Publishing to LinkedIn, idempotently
sections.content:
An author can share a post to LinkedIn from the post page. The view checks four things before it queues anything: the caller owns the post, it has not already been shared, it is published, and the account actually has a LinkedIn OAuth connection. If the broker is unreachable it returns 503 rather than claiming success — an earlier version set `posted_on_linkedin = True` and returned 200 without dispatching anything at all, so the UI reported a share that never happened.

The task itself is idempotent: it re-checks `posted_on_linkedin`, so a duplicate dispatch or a retry after a partial success never double-posts. It also calls `ensure_metadata` before composing the post, because the excerpt-generation task queued by the same save has no ordering guarantee against this one — without that call, a share dispatched right after creation can win the race and go out with no summary.

Which is why `posted_on_linkedin` is `read_only` in the serializer. It is the task's idempotency key; a client that could set it would permanently suppress sharing for that post.

sections.title: 13. The share carries the article, not just a link
sections.content:
A LinkedIn post that is only a headline and a URL asks the reader to leave the feed before they know whether it is worth it. So the share attaches the post's own PDF as a LinkedIn *document*, which renders in the feed as a swipeable carousel — the article is readable before anyone clicks anything.

The commentary beside it is deliberately short, because LinkedIn folds anything long behind "…see more": the title, one or two sentences from the excerpt cut on a word boundary, the canonical URL, and up to five of the post's tags as hashtags. Tags are normalised to what LinkedIn will actually link — a hashtag ends at the first character that is not a letter, digit or underscore, so `Next.js` becomes `#NextJs` rather than a linked `#Next` with an orphaned `.js` beside it.

The URL lives in the words on purpose. A post can carry a document or a link preview, never both, and LinkedIn auto-links a URL it finds in the commentary — so putting it there is what keeps the site one tap away from a share that is already showing the article.

Two code paths producing "the PDF" is how the preview and the artifact quietly drift apart.

sections.title: 15. Running it yourself
sections.content:
Both apps read their configuration from `.env`, and each ships a committed `.env.example` listing every variable. `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` is always `config.settings`; the environment is chosen by `DJANGO_ENV`, so manage.py, gunicorn, the worker and beat can never disagree about which settings they loaded.

In production, `config/settings/prod.py` raises `ImproperlyConfigured` at import time if `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` or `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is missing. A misconfigured deploy fails at boot rather than running insecure.

sections.title: Backend and frontend, from a clean checkout
sections.content:
# --- backend -------------------------------------------------------------
cd backend
cp .env.example .env          # then fill in GOOGLE_API_KEY
uv sync
uv run python manage.py migrate

# Everything at once: checks Redis, then starts the Celery worker, beat,
# Flower (task monitoring on :5555) and the Django dev server.
uv run python manage.py dev

# Or just Django. Tasks then run eagerly in-process: Milvus Lite holds a file
# lock on the vector index, so a worker and the web process cannot both
# open it.
uv run python manage.py runserver

# --- frontend ------------------------------------------------------------
cd ../frontend
cp .env.example .env.local    # API_BASE_URL points at the Django API
npm install
npm run dev

# --- checks --------------------------------------------------------------
uv run python manage.py test            # APITestCase per endpoint
uv run python manage.py check --deploy  # must be clean under DJANGO_ENV=prod

sections.content: The health endpoint reports rather than raises: each check is wrapped, and a failure becomes `{"ok": false, "error": "…"}` with a 503 overall status. A load balancer gets something cheap to probe, and an on-call engineer gets one URL that names which dependency is down.

sections.title: 16. The rules worth stealing
items: **One file talks to the backend.** Every timeout, retry, header and validation decision lives in one place instead of being re-litigated at forty call sites.
**Validate at the boundary.** A response that does not match the contract should fail where it arrives, naming the field — not render as a blank somewhere downstream.
**Tokens belong on the server.** httpOnly cookies plus a BFF removes XSS token theft and CORS configuration in the same move.
**Never dispatch a task with a bare .delay() from a signal.** It runs after commit; an exception there 500s a request whose row already saved, and the retry creates a duplicate.
**Classify errors before retrying them.** Retrying a permanent failure five times with backoff is a way to spend money slowly and learn nothing.
**Record the outcome of async work on the row itself.** Without that, a failed embedding and a successful one look identical from the outside.
**Never return an empty success for a failure.** An outage that looks like "no results" is an outage nobody reports.
**Hash the input before paying for it.** A content hash turned every re-save from a billed API call into a no-op.
**Change the selector and the serializer together.** A method field that queries unconditionally is an N+1 per row, and list endpoints are where it hurts.
**Fail at boot, not in production.** Settings that refuse to import without their secrets beat a deploy that quietly runs with DEBUG on.
